articles.title: North Korea denies being behind record $6.3bn Binance hack
articles.summary: US government agencies and cyber analysts have blamed Pyongyang for the record-breaking heist.
articles.preview: North Korea has denied claims that it was behind the record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack of cryptocurrency exchange Binance, calling the allegations "absurd rhetoric". Kim Yo Jong, a top Democratic People's Republic of Korea official and the sister of leader Kim Jong Un, said on Tuesday that the accusations are another "sinister attempt" by the US to damage Pyongyang's public image. The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the Secret Service and cyber analysts have said North Korea orchestrated the hack, which has been described as the largest in history.
articles.body:
North Korea has denied claims that it was behind the record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack of cryptocurrency exchange Binance, calling the allegations "absurd rhetoric".

Kim Yo Jong, a top Democratic People's Republic of Korea official and the sister of leader Kim Jong Un, said on Tuesday that the accusations are another "sinister attempt" by the US to damage Pyongyang's public image.

The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the Secret Service and cyber analysts have said North Korea orchestrated the hack, which has been described as the largest in history.

This is the latest hack to be linked to North Korea, which has been accused of relying on cyber-crime to help finance its sanctioned economy.

Blockchain analysts and the FBI have said the attack was led by state-backed hacking group TraderTraitor.

The FBI has called on industry partners to help block transactions involving cryptocurrency accounts linked to the group.

"The US has made a trite provocation of linking it with the Democratic People's Republic of Korea again," Kim Yo-jong, the director of North Korea's General Affairs Department, said in a statement.

"It is a grave political provocation against the DPRK that the US misleads the international public opinion as if all the cyber crimes in different parts of the world are our deeds," she said.

- Who could be behind the Binance hack and what we know so far

- Published3 days ago

But Pyongyang has been blamed for a number of major cyber attacks in recent years - accusations that it has denied.

The TraderTraitor unit, which is also known as the Lazarus Group, was blamed for a then-record $1.5bn hack of crypto exchange Bybit in 2025.

Pyongyang has systematically built its cyber operations, recruiting promising students from universities and sending them to hacker units overseen by North Korea's intelligence agency, research groups like the S Rajaratnam School of International Studies think tank have said.

The country has consistently denied such claims.

Kim Yo Jong said "it is the consistent policy stand of the DPRK government to resolutely oppose all sorts of malicious acts in cyberspace".

articles.summary: Persistent weakness in the world's second-largest economy, reeling from sluggish consumption and a prolonged property sector debt crisis, and sharp falls in tech stocks have hit investor confidence.
articles.preview: Persistent weakness in the world's second-largest economy, reeling from sluggish consumption and a prolonged property sector debt crisis, and sharp falls in tech stocks have hit investor confidence. BEIJING: Chinese regulators have rolled out a handful of measures, from conducting swap operations to upgrading a lending facility for stock buybacks by listed companies, as part of efforts to stabilise struggling capital markets.
articles.body:
Persistent weakness in the world's second-largest economy, reeling from sluggish consumption and a prolonged property sector debt crisis, and sharp falls in tech stocks have hit investor confidence.

BEIJING: Chinese regulators have rolled out a handful of measures, from conducting swap operations to upgrading a lending facility for stock buybacks by listed companies, as part of efforts to stabilise struggling capital markets.

Authorities also prodded index heavyweights and leading tech firms to try to stabilise their share prices, and are studying plans to ease margin rules to increase market liquidity.

China's central bank and securities watchdog made their announcements on Monday (Nov 2) after the benchmark CSI300 Index slumped 8.5 per cent in October, its worst month since early 2016.

Persistent weakness in the world's second-largest economy, reeling from sluggish consumption and a prolonged property sector debt crisis, and sharp falls in tech stocks have hit investor confidence.

Local media first reported that regulators had met with financial institutions on Monday to discuss tools to support capital markets. Share prices regained ground on Monday in expectation of supportive policies.

As part of the measures, the People's Bank of China (PBOC) said on Monday it would conduct swap operations with financial institutions on Tuesday that could inject more than 100 billion yuan (US$15 billion) into the stock market.

It will be the third time the PBOC has used the liquidity tool, created two years ago to allow brokers, insurers and fund companies to obtain liquidity for stock purchases.

The PBOC also said a relending scheme designed to fund share buybacks and purchases would shift from a temporary arrangement to a long-term mechanism. The interest rate of the expanded scheme was cut to 1 per cent from 1.25 per cent.

In a separate statement, the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) urged key index constituents and "dragon head" tech companies to "actively buy back shares" and stabilize market value. The regulator will also prod some newly established exchange-traded funds to "speed up building stock positions", and encourage fund managers to buy shares in a down-cycle.

The new round of PBOC swap operations "sends another strong signal of policymakers’ commitment to safeguarding capital market stability and supporting investor confidence", said Hao Zhou, a Hong Kong-based analyst at Guotai Haitong Securities. He said global volatility and external uncertainties continued to weigh on investor sentiment.

The PBOC said bidding under the Securities, Funds and Insurance Companies Swap Facility would take place on Tuesday.

It said 31 brokers and fund companies had already applied for swaps worth more than 100 billion yuan.

The central bank previously conducted such operations in October 2024 and January 2025, injecting a combined 105 billion yuan into the market.

The Shanghai Composite Index climbed 1.1 per cent on Monday, its biggest one-day percentage gain since Aug 27.

The CSI300 and the Shanghai Composite Index both dropped roughly 1 per cent in early trade, giving up Monday's gains.

“These measures were below expectations," said Chen Jiande, fund manager at Fujian Tianlang Asset Management Co.

"Many investors in battered tech shares are taking advantage of any rebound to rush out."

The tech-focused STAR Composite Index dropped 1.6 per cent.

Investors also remain jittery over the financial health of state-owned developer Zhuhai Huafa Group, after media reported it was seeking extensions on some bank loans.

Government bond yields held steady in early trade, with the 10-year and 30-year notes edging down about 0.3 basis points each.

articles.title: Man guilty of stealing cash from farm owned by South African president
articles.summary: The case, part of the "Farmgate" scandal, has left President Cyril Ramaphosa mired in an impeachment saga.
articles.preview: A court in South Africa has found a man guilty of stealing more than $500,000 (£372,822) in cash from a farm owned by South African president Cyril Ramaphosa, in a case that mired the head of state in an impeachment saga. Imanuwela David was found guilty of theft on Monday, as well as conspiracy to commit housebreaking with intent to steal at Phala Phala farm in the Limpopo province in 2020. Froliana Joseph, a cleaner at the property, was also found guilty of conspiracy to commit housebreaking with intent to steal.
articles.body:
A court in South Africa has found a man guilty of stealing more than $500,000 (£372,822) in cash from a farm owned by South African president Cyril Ramaphosa, in a case that mired the head of state in an impeachment saga.

Imanuwela David was found guilty of theft on Monday, as well as conspiracy to commit housebreaking with intent to steal at Phala Phala farm in the Limpopo province in 2020.

Froliana Joseph, a cleaner at the property, was also found guilty of conspiracy to commit housebreaking with intent to steal.

Her brother, Ndilinasho Joseph, was acquitted on all charges.

David was accused of breaking into the cattle farm in February 2020 and taking $580,000 (£432,000) in cash from a sofa on the property. David then went on a spending spree, buying a range of cars including three Mercedes - among them one for his girlfriend - a Porsche, two Volkswagens as well as diamond-encrusted Rolex watches and a house.

David told the court he had made the money through businesses including diamonds and Bitcoin, claims the court rejected. The court also found that David was the only one of the two convicted who had any of the stolen cash in his bank account.

Pre-sentencing will take place on 13 November.

There have been many twists and turns in what is known as the Farmgate scandal.

The theft was largely unknown until 2022 when it was brought to light by Arthur Fraser, South Africa's former intelligence chief and an ally for the former president Jacob Zuma, when he claimed that Ramaphosa hid the theft from the police and tax authorities.

Ramaphosa admitted the theft took place but denied any wrongdoing.

An independent panel that same year found Ramaphosa could have questions to answer over the burglary. MPs voted against establishing an impeachment inquiry.

In May this year, the constitutional court ruled that parliament had acted unlawfully by shelving the panel's report, and in July Ramaphosa blocked the parliamentary inquiry through a provincial court.

articles.title: Indonesian police name suspects after 58 citizens lured to Russia to serve as mercenaries
articles.summary: The Indonesian citizens were initially offered jobs in logistics, border security and defence construction, but when arriving in Russia, were told to sign contracts to serve as mercenaries, undergo training and potentially be deployed to conflict zones.
articles.preview: The Indonesian citizens were initially offered jobs in logistics, border security and defence construction, but when arriving in Russia, were told to sign contracts to serve as mercenaries, undergo training and potentially be deployed to conflict zones. JAKARTA: Indonesian authorities have uncovered a human trafficking syndicate involving 58 citizens who were allegedly recruited to work as mercenaries in Russia.
articles.body:
The Indonesian citizens were initially offered jobs in logistics, border security and defence construction, but when arriving in Russia, were told to sign contracts to serve as mercenaries, undergo training and potentially be deployed to conflict zones.

JAKARTA: Indonesian authorities have uncovered a human trafficking syndicate involving 58 citizens who were allegedly recruited to work as mercenaries in Russia.

Thirteen people have been named as suspects, including two Russians and a Ukrainian citizen, the National Police Criminal Investigation Department (Bareskrim Polri) said on Monday (Nov 2).

Nurul Azizah, director of Bareskrim Polri's directorate of crimes against women and children and human trafficking, said at a press conference that the perpetrators used social media, job portals and messaging apps to lure victims with promises of lucrative overseas employment, state news agency Antara reported.

“We are coordinating through the Indonesian National Police’s International Relations Division and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Everything is still under further review,” Nurul said in response to CNA's queries on Tuesday.

The victims were initially offered jobs in logistics, border security and defence construction, but after going through the recruitment process and being dispatched to Russia, they would be directed to sign contracts to serve as mercenaries, undergo training and potentially be deployed to conflict zones.

“It is true that they did not directly offer jobs as mercenaries, but rather as logistics workers,” Nurul told reporters in Jakarta on Monday, as quoted by Kompas.

The victims were promised signing bonuses of up to US$35,000 and monthly salaries of around US$3,000.

Rita Wulandari Wibowo, director of Women and Child Protection at Metro Jaya Regional Police, said that recruiters also promised some victims child allowances of more than 3 million rupiah along with other benefits, Kompas reported.

“But in reality, none of these promises were fulfilled; the actual values were significantly lower, with some victims yet to receive any payments to this day,” Rita said on Monday.

The 58 individuals were identified after five police reports were made. Bareskrim Polri, together with the West Jakarta Metropolitan Police, Metro Jaya Regional Police and the Bogor Police, are investigating.

In a case investigated by the Bogor Police, victims were temporarily housed at a facility in Sukamantri Village in Bogor, with two suspects, identified by the initials FIK and STH, responsible for overseeing the victims’ living arrangements while they awaited departure.

Another suspect identified as MBH served as the financier throughout this process, covering recruitment expenses, lodging fees, medical check-ups, daily food costs and travelling arrangements, Kompas reported.

articles.summary: Nearly 1,600 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza since a US-brokered 'ceasefire' took effect in October last year.

articles.body:
Nearly 1,600 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza since a US-brokered ‘ceasefire’ took effect in October last year.

Israeli forces have killed at least four Palestinians in attacks across Gaza, while a fifth person died of wounds sustained in an earlier assault, according to medical sources and media reports.

At least two people were killed in a gun attack and an air raid on southern Khan Younis on Monday, while a third was killed in a drone attack on the central al-Musaddar village, medical sources said.

The fourth person died in a strike on a vehicle in northern Gaza City’s Tal al-Hawa neighbourhood, according to the Wafa news agency. It identified the victim as Hani Hamed Kahil and said five others were wounded in the attack.

The Israeli military said it targeted Palestinian fighters in three strikes, but provided no further details.

Wafa reported that a fifth person, Youssef Abu Younis, also died of injuries sustained in an Israeli attack on a police post in al-Mawasi on Sunday. His death brought the number of deaths reported on Monday to five.

Earlier, at least five Palestinian police officers were killed in an attack on Sunday.

Elsewhere in Gaza City, three Palestinians were wounded on Monday when a minibus belonging to a community kitchen was hit in Zeitoun.

According to the Palestinian Ministry of Health, Israeli attacks have killed at least 1,593 Palestinians since the United States-brokered “ceasefire” began in October 2025, and wounded 5,748 others. Overall, Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has killed at least 74,609 Palestinians and wounded 175,872 people.

The latest attacks came amid efforts to secure shelter for displaced Palestinians before winter.

Israeli Army Radio reported that Nickolay Mladenov, the high representative of the Board of Peace, established by the US to oversee a so-called peace plan in Gaza, arrived in Israel on Monday to seek permission to bring in tents and push for steps to accelerate reconstruction.

The scale of the need in Gaza remains vast. The United Nations migration agency said on October 9 that nearly two million people required shelter assistance and half of Gaza’s tents and makeshift shelters needed replacing, leaving families exposed as winter approached.

Israeli soldiers arrest Al Jazeera journalist in Hebron raids

Israeli forces have arrested Al Jazeera Arabic’s correspondent Montaser Nassar in a raid on his home in the southern occupied West Bank.

Nassar was arrested early on Tuesday at his home in Dura, near the city of Hebron.

Video of the arrest shows Israeli forces leading Nassar, who was blindfolded and handcuffed, into a military vehicle.

Nassar was among more than 13 Palestinians arrested in Dura on Tuesday, sources told Al Jazeera. All were taken to an undisclosed location.

Israeli forces had previously assaulted Nassar and his cameraman in Dura on December 29, 2023, causing bruising.

The arrest comes amid mounting pressure on Palestinian journalists in the occupied West Bank. The Palestinian Journalists Syndicate recorded 84 alleged press violations by Israeli forces and settlers in August alone, including arrests and a death in custody.

articles.title: Russian bombing kills 26 people at Ukraine aid centre, Kyiv says
articles.summary: Officials say at least nine 3,000kg aerial bombs hit a southern Ukrainian village in what the president called an "utterly horrific" attack.
articles.preview: At least 26 people were killed after Russian bombs hit an aid distribution centre, in an attack that Ukraine's leader has called "utterly horrific". Five people were injured and 27 initially reported missing after at least nine 3,000kg aerial bombs hit the village of Komyshuvakha in the southern Zaporizhzhia region, regional head Mykhailo Semikin said. President Volodymyr Zelensky said that after the first strike on the local school "used for humanitarian needs", there was a second attack on the place where people were sheltering.
articles.body:
At least 26 people were killed after Russian bombs hit an aid distribution centre, in an attack that Ukraine's leader has called "utterly horrific".

Five people were injured and 27 initially reported missing after at least nine 3,000kg aerial bombs hit the village of Komyshuvakha in the southern Zaporizhzhia region, regional head Mykhailo Semikin said.

President Volodymyr Zelensky said that after the first strike on the local school "used for humanitarian needs", there was a second attack on the place where people were sheltering.

He posted a video showing a huge crater left after Monday's attack, and rescuer teams searching through the rubble.

The Russian military has not publicly commented.

Zelensky initially put the death toll at 18, but Ukraine's state emergencies service DSNS later said 24 people, including two rescuers and four police officers, were confirmed to have been killed.

In his video address late on Monday, Zelensky said 26 people were now known to have died.

He earlier said that "the Russians could not have been unaware that the local residents who remained in Komyshuvakha received humanitarian aid there every week" on Monday.

"This is yet another proof that Russia does not want any de-escalation."

He said that after a recent successful joint Russian-Ukrainian operation to evacuate civilians from the Russia-occupied southern city of Oleshky during a temporary ceasefire brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump, "there was a moment when the next steps could show that peace is possible".

"With such killings, Russia is sending the exact opposite signal - Russia is counting on further killings," Zelensky said.

Meanwhile, Semikin described the Russian attack as a "terrible tragedy" for the village, confirming that "people are still under the rubble".

He said rescue teams were working at the scene, but they had been forced to halt their operation a number of times because of Russian drone attacks in the area.

A day of mourning has been declared for Tuesday across the entire Zaporizhzhia region.

Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Teams from Ukraine, Russia and the US are due to resume peace talks in Abu Dhabi, the United Arab Emirates, next week, US President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff said on X.

Since the talks were suspended in February, Moscow has stepped up attacks as Kyiv virtually ran out of Western-supplied interceptors to defend against missiles.

No major breakthrough is expected at the talks. Witkoff said the discussions would focus on "post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian efforts, and next steps toward peace".

Witkoff said US negotiators would also meet European and Nato officials this week in Brussels.

articles.preview: Ukrainian president Zelenskyy says attack on aid hub was ‘vile’ and shows Russia does not want to de-escalate Russia on Monday bombed an aid distribution centre and neighbouring shelter in southern Ukraine, killing at least 26 ​people, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy and the country’s emergency services said. Emergency services said two members of a rescue crew and four police officers were among the dead in the village ⁠of Komyshuvakha, in south-eastern Zaporizhzhia region.
articles.body:
Russia on Monday bombed an aid distribution centre and neighbouring shelter in southern Ukraine, killing at least 26 people, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy and the country’s emergency services said.

Emergency services said two members of a rescue crew and four police officers were among the dead in the village of Komyshuvakha, in south-eastern Zaporizhzhia region. Five people were being treated in hospital, including two rescue workers.

Zelenskyy, in his nightly video address, said Russian forces initially dropped bombs on a school in the village that was used as a shelter and for distributing humanitarian assistance.

There were no classes at the school, he said, as the village, lying south-east of the region’s main city, also called Zaporizhzhia, was too close to the frontline.

“The Russians struck first just as people were arriving – a few aerial bombs,” he said. “Then there was a second strike – more air bombs, this time on the shelter. A vile terrorist strike.”

As night fell in Komyshuvakha, emergency responders used torches to search through the rubble of collapsed buildings, according to photos and video posted online by local officials. Regina Kharchenko, secretary of the Zaporizhzhia city council, said that 27 people were missing in the attack.

Efforts to rescue people Monday evening were hindered as Russian drones launched additional attacks in the area that had been bombed, according to Mykhailo Semikin, a military official in Zaporizhzhia.

Zelenskyy said the Russians could not have been unaware that residents remaining in Komyshuvakha gathered each week to pick up humanitarian packages from the site.

The attack, he said, had shown that Moscow was intent on killing people instead of building on the past week’s ceasefire in the embattled southern city of Oleshky, brokered by US first lady Melania Trump.

“Russians continue to demonstrate, time and again, their hatred of Ukraine and everything that exists here,” he said.

“If Russia genuinely wanted de-escalation, there was an opportunity following the situation in Oleshky to continue taking humanitarian steps. We proposed this. But Russia continues to kill people.”

The ceasefire last week enabled an evacuation of the Russian-occupied Oleshky.

It was the longest pause in fighting between the neighbours in the war, now in its fifth year, which has killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions.

The Kremlin said that no other similar missions were being planned “at the moment”.

US-led talks between Russia and Ukraine are set to resume next week, US special envoy Steve Witkoff said on Monday.

President Donald Trump has pushed for a settlement to the dragging war but there has been no breakthrough.

The talks – to be held 10 November and 11 in Abu Dhabi, Witkoff said – come as Kyiv and its European allies worry that Trump has increasingly sided with Moscow.

*With Reuters, Associated Press and Agence France-Presse

articles.title: Thousands of European troops to rehearse Ukraine deployment in event of peace
articles.summary: Western officials stress that any force sent to Ukraine would not take part in any offensive operations.
articles.preview: Britain and France are to lead a military exercise to test a multinational force's ability to deploy to Ukraine, if there is a peace deal. Nearly 3,000 military personnel from 12 European nations will take part in the rehearsal in neighbouring Poland this month. Plans for a reassurance force for Ukraine were set out last year as one of the long-term security guarantees being proposed by European nations. But there are still more questions than answers as to how such a military force might work in practice.
articles.body:
Britain and France are to lead a military exercise to test a multinational force's ability to deploy to Ukraine, if there is a peace deal.

Nearly 3,000 military personnel from 12 European nations will take part in the rehearsal in neighbouring Poland this month.

Plans for a reassurance force for Ukraine were set out last year as one of the long-term security guarantees being proposed by European nations.

But there are still more questions than answers as to how such a military force might work in practice. Western officials stress that any force sent to Ukraine would not take part in offensive operations or be involved in peacekeeping or ceasefire monitoring missions.

Nor would they be operating under the command of Nato or on the front line.

Officials say their presence would be to provide reassurance to Ukraine and to help rebuild its armed forces.

The US has been involved in discussions, but is not contributing to the mission.

Russia has already voiced opposition to foreign troops being stationed in Ukraine and, last year, President Vladimir Putin said they would be "legitimate targets".

Western officials have declined to spell out the rules of engagement if any international troops were to be attacked in Ukraine. Though they say the force would be able to defend itself.

UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the exercise showed Britain, France and their allies were stepping up preparation for the day when peace came to Ukraine.

He said: "This is not a hypothetical plan, it's a real force, ready to help Ukraine once the fighting stops."

Lt Gen Tom Bateman, the UK commander of the Multi National Force â Ukraine (MNF-U), said the exercise represented an important step in translating political commitments into credible military readiness.

He said it was a "real, capable, readily deployable force that represented a serious commitment from Coalition of the Willing nations to Ukraine's long-term stability and security".

Exercise Koalicja - which takes place from 9-22 November - will be a rehearsal of how to move, protect and supply a force in Ukraine. It will also be a test of their command and control to ensure troops from different countries can work together.

Some 2,800 military personnel will take part across land, sea and air, with the UK contribution including 300 troops and a pair of RAF Typhoons.

Fighter jets will simulate how they would reassure commercial aircraft once Ukraine's skies can be reopened.

Turkey has agreed to lead the maritime mission, with the eventual goal to clear mines and allow the resumption of trade in the Black Sea.

As well as the UK, troops will come from France, Belgium, Estonia, France, Germany, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Poland, Spain, Sweden, and Turkey.

However, Western officials could not comment on the final make-up and shape of the force that could be deployed to Ukraine if the fighting stops.

In the past, military experts have suggested that Western nations might have to send tens of thousands of troops to Ukraine to guarantee its security.

Officials acknowledge that the countries' commitment and contributions will depend on the circumstances of a cessation of hostilities and individual nations' political decisions.

It is also unclear what training role Western forces could provide to battle hardened Ukraine.

Ukrainian soldiers are already in high demand training Nato forces - passing on their expertise in drone warfare.

Above all, Russia has shown no sign of wanting to end its war.

Iranian missiles that struck U.S. military bases and Gulf energy facilities in the last round of fighting exposed a vulnerability at the heart of Washington’s decades-old security architecture. articles.title: US elections 2026: Can a Democrat-controlled Senate thwart Trump's agenda?
articles.summary: US elections 2026: Can a Democrat-controlled Senate thwart Trump's agenda? Submitted by Yasmine El-Sabawi on Mon, 11/02/2026 - 16:31 In short: Maybe, and much of it will centre on how debates are framed moving forward Voters cast their ballots at a polling station inside a shopping mall in Anchorage, Alaska, on 2 November 2026, a day ahead of the US midterm elections (Charly Triballeau/AFP) Off American voters are fed up, as almost every conversation with them will demonstrate, regardless of party affiliation. In the lead-up to the 3 November midterm elections, early voting has seen an unprecedented turnout of 56 million Americans, a stunning figure considering non-presidential election years have traditionally had low turnout rates. President Donald Trump's approval rating is lower than that of his last three predecessors when their first midterm election season rolled around, including his own first term in office. If both the polling and the predictions of Republican analysts are anything to go by, Democrats will not only retake the House after Tuesday's midterm elections, but also take the powerful Senate, and boast the most governors across the 50 states. But there may be little change in actual legislation, and a lot more change in narrative and framing in the US legislature. Rina Shah, a former Republican congressional adviser, told Middle East Eye that in the Senate, the workable strategy will be refusal - not reversal - of administration policy. For example, as Trump and his party try to appoint conservative judges to federal courts, liberal senators could block them. articles.summary: Il sottosegretario Mantovano vedrà anche l'Agenzia per la Cybersicurezza dopo i casi in Sicilia. Problemi in Belgio, Svezia e altri Paesi. Tonnellate di cibo a rischio
articles.preview: "In alcuni punti vendita Coop, almeno tre a Catania e uno a Palermo, si sono verificati attacchi hacker ai sistemi di refrigerazione dei banchi alimentari". articles.body:
"In alcuni punti vendita Coop, almeno tre a Catania e uno a Palermo, si sono verificati attacchi hacker ai sistemi di refrigerazione dei banchi alimentari". Lo dice Giuseppe Spadaro direttore generale del gruppo Radenza, che gestisce supermercati a marchio Coop. L'attacco, aggiunge, ha portato alla modifica dei parametri della temperatura surruiscaldando i banchi e provocando un deperimento degli alimenti. La polizia postale sta ricostruendo la provenienza degli attacchi e l'entità e sta verificando se vi siano o meno collegamenti con quanto accaduto in altri Paesi europei. L'attacco è avvenuto alle 4 del mattino - aggiunge Spadaro - Stiamo calcolando i danni. In alcuni casi abbiamo risolto. Abbiamo già contattato l'Agenzia per la cybersicurezza nazionale e attivato i protocolli per fare indagini in profondità".

Domani (martedì 3 novembre 2026) alle ore 11.30, si terrà a Palazzo Chigi una riunione, coordinata dal Sottosegretario alla Presidenza del Consiglio Alfredo Mantovano, per fare il punto sull'ondata di attacchi. Parteciperanno il Direttore dell'Agenzia per la Cybersicurezza Nazionale e i Direttori delle Agenzie di intelligence.

Il punto in Europa alle 18:40 (ora italiana)

(di Mattia B. Bagnoli)

Un filo rosso ormai collega gli attacchi hacker ai refrigeratori dei supermercati che si stanno moltiplicando in Europa, seguendo il modello di quanto accaduto in Francia lo scorso 12 ottobre. Ora resta semmai da capire dove porteranno le indagini, per scoprire chi li ha ordinati e come ha agito, anche per evitare nuove sorprese in futuro. A segnalare gravi anomalie - con i freezer improvvisamente tramutati in forni, viste le temperature schizzate a 50 gradi sopra lo zero - sono state catene della grande distribuzione in Belgio, Svezia, Lussemburgo, Estonia, Olanda e Irlanda. Uno sviluppo che l'Unione Europea ha definito "altamente preoccupante". I disservizi sono scattati nella notte, con l'amara scoperta dopo l'apertura.

"Stiamo svuotando i congelatori, non c'è molto altro che possiamo fare", ha commentato Dennis Vidal, responsabile di uno dei negozi nel sud della Svezia colpiti dal problema. "Stanno ricominciando a raffreddarsi ma è già tutto rovinato", ha sottolineato alla tv pubblica Svt. Vista l'entità del danno, si temono tonnellate di derrate alimentari da buttare in mezza Europa. In Belgio a segnalare "incidenti informatici" sono stati colossi come Delhaize, Carrefour, Intermarché e Spar, in decine di punti vendita, sia nelle Fiandre che in Vallonia. Gli hacker, anche in questo caso, hanno attivato a distanza la modalità di sbrinamento degli impianti, facendo salire la temperatura dei frigoriferi e dei congelatori al di sopra dei limiti previsti dalla legge. La procura federale belga ha avviato un'indagine ma non ha fornito ulteriori dettagli.

Dal canto suo, il Centro per la Sicurezza Informatica del Belgio (CCB) ha espresso preoccupazione per l'aumento del numero d'incidenti, dovuto in particolare all'uso mirato dell'intelligenza artificiale (IA), tendenza in accelerazione negli ultimi sei mesi. "Si tratta di un tentativo deliberato d'interrompere la nostra catena di approvvigionamento alimentare e di minare la fiducia dei consumatori: un monito che dobbiamo prendere sul serio", ha evidenziato il commissario all'agricoltura, Christophe Hansen assicurando che solleverà la "questione con i miei colleghi commissari nella nostra prossima riunione" del collegio. "Questi episodi dimostrano che gli attacchi informatici possono interrompere i servizi, avere ripercussioni sulle imprese e incidere direttamente sulla vita quotidiana dei cittadini", ha rimarcato un portavoce della Commissione Europea. "L'Ue - ha ricordato - dispone di diversi strumenti per rispondere a tali episodi". Nessuno, al momento, ha però rivendicato gli attacchi, benché ci siano pochi dubbi sulla natura coordinata degli incidenti.

"Si tratta di cyberattacco, non c'è altra spiegazione", ha assicurato il portavoce di Carrefour Belgio Mich Vergauwen (i disagi si sono verificati in una quindicina dei 700 negozi della catena presenti nel Paese). Il gruppo belga di refrigerazione industriale Sabcobel ha precisato di aver iniziato a mettere in sicurezza i propri impianti dopo l'attacco del 12 ottobre in Francia ma che circa il 10% dei macchinari non era ancora stato sottoposto a revisione e che alcuni si trovavano proprio nei negozi colpiti. Stando ad una prima valutazione, se si incrociano i dati, emerge come cruciale il tema dell'aggiornamento, poiché i sistemi finiti nel mirino sembrano essere quelli più anziani - ad esempio collegati alla rete 4G invece che alla più moderna 5G - o non sufficientemente schermati. A seguito dell'attacco in Francia, il produttore danese Danfoss aveva non a caso spiegato che le apparecchiature malfunzionanti, nella maggior parte dei casi, erano prodotti obsoleti ormai incapaci di ricevere "aggiornamenti software o di sicurezza".

"Imminente attacco nucleare, rischio radiazioni, trovate un rifugio": sono i messaggi di allerta spuntati nella notte nelle app di allarme antiaereo sui telefoni di ucraini e russi, dopo un massiccio cyber attacco. Fake news a cui però hanno fatto seguito, appena finita la tregua per Oleshky, nuove stragi.

"Attacco russo assolutamente devastante contro l'abitato di Komyshuvakha, nella regione di Zaporizhzhia. Dalle prime ore di questa mattina, il centro abitato è stato colpito più volte da bombe aeree". Lo denuncia su X il presidente ucraino, Volodymyr Zelensky. "Gli attacchi hanno preso di mira una scuola utilizzata per attività umanitarie, dove le persone stavano ricevendo aiuti umanitari", ha spiegato Zelensky, aggiungendo che si continuano a cercare "eventuali dispersi".

Il Servizio statale per le emergenze ucraino ha riferito che il numero delle vittime del raid aereo russo su Komyshuvas è di 24 morti, tra cui 2 soccorritori e 4 agenti di polizia. Altre 5 persone sono rimaste ferite, tra cui 2 soccorritori. Lo scrive la Ukrainska Pravda. Il capo dell'amministrazione militare di Zaporizhzhia, Mykhailo Semikin, ha riferito che gli occupanti russi hanno colpito il centro del villaggio con almeno nove bombe guidate Fab-3000. Ci sono più di venti dispersi.

Altre vittime si contano a Izyum e nella regione di Kherson. Ore prima, i sistemi di allerta mobile erano andati in tilt: "Ciao! Ci sarà una minaccia nucleare su tutta l'Ucraina. Non preoccupatevi, l'Oreshnik sta arrivando", recitava uno dei messaggi più fragorosi, con riferimento al micidiale missile balistico russo a medio raggio. E ancora: "Ci sono scontri in strada a Kiev, non uscite di casa", oppure "c'è una allerta chimica", e così via. Alcuni però erano scritti in russo, come quello che citava l'Orenshnik, quindi in tanti hanno capito subito che qualcosa non andava, non foss'altro perché un missile nucleare lanciato su Kiev scatenerebbe probabilmente la terza, e ultima, guerra mondiale. Altri sono invece rimasti letteralmente scioccati, per lunghissimi minuti di angoscia che devono essere sembrati ore. Poi è arrivata la comunicazione ufficiale delle autorità, che confermava la violazione di sicurezza. Una manciata di ore dopo tocca alla Russia: il ministero per le situazioni di emergenza comunica che l'app per avvisare la popolazione in caso di attacchi aerei è stata colpita da un "massiccio attacco informatico che ha consentito ai pirati informatici di inviare informazioni false alla popolazione".

Anche in questo caso di un attacco di droni ucraini ad alta velocità P1-Sun, anch'essi armati con testate nucleari. La violazione è scattata verso le 3 del mattino ora locale, colpendo con falsi allarmi "33 regioni russe su 89", secondo i dati del ministero. A quanto si apprende, non quella di Mosca, dove i messaggi non sono arrivati, certamente non su larga scala.

Il portavoce del Cremlino Dmitry Peskov con la sua tradizionale flemma ha sminuito il tutto: "Succede tutti i giorni, viene attaccato anche il sito della presidenza". Fonti vicine al Cremlino affermano di aver avuto una rivendicazione dell'attacco da parte di un collettivo hacker, Hitcore, che però non è particolarmente conosciuto e non è nella lista dei principali gruppi più pericolosi, anche se gli esperti ammoniscono che l'avvento dell'Ia potrebbe aumentare le capacità aggressive di gruppi poco articolati. A Oleshky intanto si è conclusa la tregua: "La missione è stata un successo, fornendo aiuti essenziali alla regione e consentendo l'evacuazione di quasi 800 persone", ha reclamato la First lady americana, Melania Trump: "Spero che serva da base per una pace duratura tra le due nazioni".

Il commissario ucraino per i diritti umani Dmytro Lubinets, e la collega russa, Yana Lantratova, hanno concordato di rivolgere un appello alla First lady statunitense per estendere la missione umanitaria da Oleshky ad altri insediamenti in situazioni di difficoltà. Sullo sfondo, rivela il Wall Street Journal, gli Usa sostengono una rapida ripresa delle vendite di gas naturale russo verso l'Europa tramite gasdotti che attraversano l'Ucraina nell'ambito dei negoziati per ottenere una tregua energetica per l'inverno. Steve Witkoff e Jared Kushenr "hanno paventato l'idea durante il loro viaggio in Russia e Ucraina in settembre". La vendita sarebbe realizzata tramite un intermediario americano per aggirare le sanzioni.

Il Cremlino non smentisce ma frena: "La ripresa del transito del gas russo verso l'Europa attraverso l'Ucraina è al momento quasi impossibile", ha commentato il solito Peskov, concedendo che "le prospettive dipenderanno dalla volontà e dalle capacità sia dei venditori che degli acquirenti".

articles.title: Fake nuclear warning from hacked app sparks unease but not panic in Ukraine
articles.summary: Many Ukrainians, who have faced years of Russian attacks, did not take the messages seriously and doubted their veracity.
articles.preview: Ukrainians have grown weary of the relentless alerts blaring from their phones and echoing through their streets, day and night, warning of Russian drones and missiles. On Sunday night, the system delivered something to make them sit up and take note â a succession of more extreme threats that quickly escalated to impending nuclear strikes, chemical attacks and combat on the streets. But many in the country did not take them seriously and doubted the veracity of the messages.
articles.body:
Ukrainians have grown weary of the relentless alerts blaring from their phones and echoing through their streets, day and night, warning of Russian drones and missiles.

On Sunday night, the system delivered something to make them sit up and take note â a succession of more extreme threats that quickly escalated to impending nuclear strikes, chemical attacks and combat on the streets.

But many in the country did not take them seriously and doubted the veracity of the messages.

Sofia Kochmar, 34, a mother-of-one living in the western city of Lviv, said she was initially concerned but quickly questioned the authenticity of the alerts.

"The first thing I saw was the word 'nuclear' and that made me pretty nervous and scared. So my first thought was that something nuclear was actually flying toward us."

"But then the notification mentioned 'street fighting in Kyiv', and I thought, wait, no, that's impossible."

The alerts included some messages written in Russian, and one included a link to a Telegram channel apparently owned by a hacker group.

Within 15 minutes, Ukraine's Air Force issued a statement saying the alert app had been compromised and clarifying there was no radiation threat. But it took more than an hour to issue "all clear" messages.

Anastasiia Romanytska, a 29-year-old ballerina living in Kyiv, said she does not have the alert app installed but friends forwarded her the warnings.

"My first reaction was, 'Is this some kind of joke?' But then my body reacted as if I was under stress. My heart started racing, and my stomach tightened up."

"Still, somehow I immediately realised that it wasn't something serious. Or maybe I just really wanted to believe that."

There are a number of apps delivering phone notifications of air raid warnings, with maps showing areas under threat, all using the same data as the official government-backed app.

Yevhen Baliutov, a cybersecurity expert at Kyiv School of Economics, told the BBC it was clear to him the Ukrainian alert system was hacked by Russians, saying many Ukrainians had clicked a link included with the alerts leading to a Russian Telegram channel, potentially exposing them to further disinformation, phishing attempts or data breaches.

"This is a war, so it's no surprise that Russia will try to hack, will try to send us fake news, will try to manipulate, and will use that for their propaganda."

While both Russia and Ukraine are widely believed to carry out cyberattacks against one another, the informal language used in the hoax alerts on Sunday pointed to so-called hacktivist groups, which could be aligned to Moscow or Kyiv but are not formally directed by either government.

Baliutov said it was also logical that Ukraine would have responded by launching a cyber-attack on the Russian emergency alert system. Both sides have similar capabilities in cyber warfare, he added.

Kochmar said after the initial concern, Ukrainians quickly turned to joking about the incident.

"All our work group chats immediately blew up. Everyone started messaging each other, discussing what was happening. And what I found fascinating was how quickly we turned the whole thing into a joke."

Although the impact of this incident had been limited, it illustrated the weakness of a crucial system, Baliutov said.

"It's very dangerous for Ukraine and for our people. When developing such applications, we need to consider security from the very beginning, without skipping essential security measures. When millions of people rely on a service, we cannot afford to take shortcuts with security."

The authorities already faced the challenge of maintaining public alertness after four and a half years of war with ceaseless attack warnings sounding sometimes hourly. Now they must reassure people the systems in place to protect them are robust, trustworthy and should be followed.

articles.body:
The oil price has fallen to its lowest level in more two weeks amid new hopes of a breakthrough to end the Iran war.

Brent crude, the international benchmark, dropped by more than 6.5% to as low as $105.55 a barrel on Monday, the lowest since 16 October, sending shares in airline companies higher and pushing down government borrowing costs.

Oil prices fell after Tehran revealed that contacts between Iran and the US to end their eight-month war were continuing.

“Consultations through mediators are very intensive. We have presented our conditions and proposals and everything depends on the political rationality of Washington,” the Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said, according to the state media outlet IRNA.

Over the weekend, Qatari officials tried to negotiate the release of more than $6bn (£4.5bn) in Iranian assets, so that Tehran might allow the strait of Hormuz to reopen.

On Monday, US vice-president JD Vance reported that there had been “a number of good conversations with the Iranians” and that he was feeling good about the prospects of a “negotiated settlement”.

Vance sent a letter to Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, last week but the White House has offered few details about the contents of that correspondence.

Donald Trump had earlier taken a belligerent tone, telling voters in Iowa on Sunday that Iran would receive “the hammer” unless there was progress.

“The only reason why I’m not finished with Iran is I want to be nice. I want to try and save all those lives if I can ... But at some point we’re going to have to give them the hammer,” he said during a campaign rally in the run-up to the US midterm elections.

But investors were cheered by reports on Monday that Iran’s supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, had granted “powers” to his government in its talks with the US seeking to end the Middle East war.

Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said: “The news is manna from heaven for stock markets, which have felt increasingly pressured by oil’s rise, but of course there is still a risk that Trump will try one last throw of the iron dice after the midterms.”

The drop in the oil price sparked hopes of a break in the inflationary pressures gripping the global economy. Government borrowing costs dropped, with the yield – or interest rate – on 10-year UK bonds down 10 basis points, or 0.1 of a percentage point, to the lowest since 22 September.

Shares in British Airways’ parent company, IAG, rose by 4.2% in London, while United Airlines jumped 7% in New York.

articles.title: China calls for Mideast dialogue in talks with Iran, Saudi, Oman
articles.summary: "All parties should ... in a spirit of reason and pragmatism, focus on a political solution rather than once again resorting to armed conflict," said Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi.
articles.preview: "All parties should ... in a spirit of reason and pragmatism, focus on a political solution rather than once again resorting to armed conflict," said Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi. BEIJING: China stepped up diplomatic efforts on Monday (Nov 2) to resolve the Middle East crisis, urging a return to the negotiating table in back-to-back meetings with Iranian, Omani and Saudi officials in Beijing.
articles.body:
"All parties should ... in a spirit of reason and pragmatism, focus on a political solution rather than once again resorting to armed conflict," said Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi.

BEIJING: China stepped up diplomatic efforts on Monday (Nov 2) to resolve the Middle East crisis, urging a return to the negotiating table in back-to-back meetings with Iranian, Omani and Saudi officials in Beijing.

The meetings come days after US President Donald Trump issued a fresh war threat more than eight months into the conflict, which was triggered by US-Israeli strikes on Iran and has at times spilled over into neighbouring countries.

Beijing supports Tehran in "safeguarding its own sovereignty and security", Foreign Minister Wang Yi told Ali Bagheri Kani, the deputy secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, according to a Chinese statement.

Wang later called for dialogue to end the conflict "while safeguarding regional energy security and the safety of shipping lanes", as he met with Saudi National Security Adviser Musaad bin Mohammad al-Aiban.

China, a top economic partner of Iran, has long sought a detente in the months-long conflict that has disrupted global shipping.

Trump said on Saturday that the United States had knocked out much of Iran's military but still has to "take care of" one or two targets, with Tehran warning of reprisals if attacked.

"All parties should ... in a spirit of reason and pragmatism, focus on a political solution rather than once again resorting to armed conflict," Wang told Bagheri Kani, according to the statement.

China's foreign ministry had not previously announced the visit by Bagheri Kani to Beijing.

President Xi Jinping also met Oman's sultan for talks in Beijing on Monday - the first visit to China by the Gulf nation's head of state since diplomatic ties were established.

Xi told Haitham bin Tariq that China was ready to "contribute to peace, stability and prosperity in the region".

The Chinese leader said that the Middle East should not become a "wrestling ground for major-country rivalry and geopolitical conflicts", state news agency Xinhua reported.

Later this month, Beijing will send its Middle East envoy to Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia as a part of "shuttle diplomacy visits ... aimed at promoting peace talks (and) easing tensions", a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson told a news briefing.

articles.title: What might Trump have planned for Iran following the midterm election?
articles.summary: While the US midterms could open a window for diplomacy with Iran, they could also unleash a new military escalation. DW spoke with analysts to identify eight factors that could tip the balance toward war or peace.
articles.preview: November 2, 2026 While the US midterms could open a window for diplomacy with Iran, they could also unleash a new military escalation. DW spoke with analysts to identify eight factors that could tip the balance toward war or peace. The US Republican Party is entering the midterm elections with Donald Trump's administration seemingly unable to either win or diplomatically resolve the Iran war.
articles.body:
November 2, 2026

While the US midterms could open a window for diplomacy with Iran, they could also unleash a new military escalation. DW spoke with analysts to identify eight factors that could tip the balance toward war or peace.

The US Republican Party is entering the midterm elections with Donald Trump's administration seemingly unable to either win or diplomatically resolve the Iran war. If the Republicans lose control of the US Congress, the administration will have to navigate an entirely different political landscape for the rest of Trump's second term, but the course of the war is not decided just in Washington — or in Tehran.

Seeking to identify key factors that could tip the balance towards war or peace in Iran, DW spoke with Omid Memarian of DAWN, a Washington-based think tank focused on reforming the US's Middle East policy; the Finland-based political scientist Leila Morovati; and Babak Rezaeedaryakenari, a professor of international relations at Leiden University in the Netherlands.

1. US midterms: Is Trump set for more scrutiny?

A Democratic victory would push Trump to focus more on domestic issues and would likely expose the financial costs of the war in the US Congress, Memarian told DW. However, Trump could continue limited strikes on Iran without formally declaring war.

Memarian said Trump would seek a way out that "saves face" after Tuesday's election.

With Trump, Memarian said, Iran is engaged in a "big gamble with someone who does not behave like a conventional politician." This increases the risk of renewed attacks.

Rezaeedaryakenari made a similar point: "The president has broad authority and freedom of action, especially in foreign policy and the conduct of military operations. A Republican defeat, even with increased pressure from Congress, doesn't necessarily stop new attacks."

2. Deadlock in Israel puts pressure on Netanyahu

Israel's October 27 election ended in deadlock. Neither the coalition around incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, nor the camp supporting former IDF chief Gadi Eisenkot managed to secure an outright majority.

Memarian said the political uncertainty could push Netanyahu to act on major decisions while he still wields power — making the transition period the "most fragile and dangerous" for renewed escalation.

A change of government in Israel would not fundamentally alter Israel's Iran policy, Memarian said. Netanyahu's main rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, "may be more deferential to America" and coordinate more closely with Washington. But ties with Trump are personal, and Eisenkot "certainly won't be like Netanyahu, who could sell any plan or scenario to Trump."

Rezaeedaryakenari said Israel's security concerns about Iran "are not limited to Netanyahu himself." A new government could change the timing of a confrontation and coordination with Washington, but the security establishment and ruling coalition would also shape the risk of an attack, he said.

3. Nuclear impasse: 'The ladder of tension'

Iran's nuclear program remains the biggest open issue between the governments, with the US rejecting the Iranian narrative that the program is meant only for civilian use.

But the two sides are also at odds on how the talks themselves should be set up, Memarian said.

"The US wants negotiations to start not only with a focus on Iran's nuclear program, but with concessions right at the outset," he said.

Iran seeks the lifting of sanctions and the release of frozen assets before nuclear talks begin. If the sides don't move closer, Memarian warns, the odds of a renewed war rise.

Until the sides agree on an agenda, Memarian said, they are likely to keep "climbing the ladder of tension."

Morovati, a Finland-based political analyst, said the nuclear program was "the crux" of the standoff. Iran's government sees it as a survival guarantee and bargaining chip, she said. In turn, Washington fears that a nuclear Iran would upend its security calculations and long-term strategy for the Middle East and beyond, which is why it insists on putting the issue on the table first.

4. Strait of Hormuz: Is Iran's leverage also a risk factor?

Before the United States and Israel launched the war in late February, about 20% of the world's oil passed through the Strait of Hormuz. Iran has since drastically cut on the energy exports through the naval chokepoint, using at as leverage on US and Israel.

But, Memarian said, Iran's restrictions in the strait won't trigger escalation on their own.

Should US officials decide that a broader attack is needed to change Iran's calculations, any incident could serve as a pretext, Memarian said. If Washington considers the risks too high, it may opt for an economic blockade while keeping negotiations on the table. In that scenario, "even occasional tensions in the Strait of Hormuz won't pull America into war," according to the US-based analyst.

5. The Houthis in Yemen: Iran's allies, not subordinates

The Houthi rebels in Yemen have also been targeting energy exports on the Red Sea — including attacks on Saudi cities and infrastructure. But Memarian notes the Yemeni rebels' roots and struggle are "entirely domestic and organic" despite their ideological closeness to Tehran.

Memarian said the Houthis made "pragmatic calculations" and their actions did not necessarily translate into an escalation between Iran and the United States.

Still, the United States could use the rebels' action as a pretext to strike Iran again.

Rezaeedaryakenari offered a slightly different assessment. Houthi attacks on shipping and on countries in the region, he says, "can both widen the war and accelerate coalition-building against the Islamic Republic." Countries that don't want war with Tehran "may turn to closer military cooperation to protect their trade and security." That doesn't necessarily mean entering the war directly, he adds, "but it could narrow the Islamic Republic's room for maneuver."

6. Regional mediators: Four countries with a lot at stake

With direct talks between the governments of Iran and the United States stalled, the world turned its attention to Qatar, Oman, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia. While each nation plays a different role in the crisis, they all have a direct stake in ending the war.

"They are close to the US, but also want to maintain ties with Iran and build regional alliances to prevent future conflicts," Memarian said.

Morovati said the failure of the United States to support its Arab allies during the war could eventually push them to reconsider their policies and turn to the US's rivals.

7. What will Trump administration do after the election?

During the campaign, Trump said he expected a deal with Iran soon after the midterm elections. Meanwhile, the Reuters news agency cited three senior Iranian officials and an additional source as saying that Tehran has deliberately prolonged talks to weaken Trump politically.

Memarian said Iran's leaders believed that a Republican defeat would increase pressure on Trump to end the war. But Trump will remain the key foreign policy decision-maker, and congressional pressure is unlikely to play a deciding role.

He said the present moment offers the "best opportunity" to end the standoff before Trump leaves office in January 2029.

"Iran's leaders need to think about their endgame," Memarian said, warning that Trump could launch a massive attack, inflict serious damage and then declare victory.

Rezaeedaryakenari said "escalatory factors" would have the upper hand in the coming months — and the likelihood of a military escalation is high.

Iran's government can only avert a new round of war with a fundamental policy shift and concessions that the country's leaders would consider close to surrender. However, he said, such a retreat would also threaten the regime's survival by weakening its ideological justification and eroding support.

8. Economic toll: Warring parties not at breaking point

High oil prices, shipping risks and economic strain are putting pressure on all sides as the war enters its ninth month. Could that push Tehran, Washington and regional capitals toward compromise?

"The economy is the Achilles' heel of every party to this war," Morovati said, "and that holds even for countries beyond the region."

Energy prices as a source of pressure on the US government, Morovati said.

"We've seen that energy supply and the expectations of the American public have been influential," Morovati said, "and this is one of the problems the Trump administration faces."

At the same time, Morovati said, Arab countries do not act as a united bloc toward Tehran.

"If they come under severe security and economic pressure, they may take joint action, but so far that hasn't happened in practice," Morovati said.

Memarian also sees the economic costs as an incentive for a deal. But he also claims that each side believes that inflicting more pain on the other will strengthen its hand in future talks.

"That can easily turn this into a war of attrition, and in recent months that has been the approach," Memarian said. Neither side has yet reached the point where it sees compromise as unavoidable.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

Russia has agreed to stop the recruitment of Ghanaian nationals to fight the war in Ukraine, Accra said in a statement.

President Putin reportedly gave the assurance on the sidelines of last week’s Russia-Africa summit in Moscow after his Ghanaian counterpart, John Mahama, raised the issue.

Ghana last month said its citizens were being "tricked" into joining the Russian war effort and urged Moscow to do more to halt the practice.

As of mid-August, more than 270 Ghanaians had fought for Russia and at least 62 have been killed in the fighting; an additional 15 are missing.

Now President Putin has said he will ban Ghanaians from participating, whether through irregular recruitment or voluntary enlistment.

Several African countries including Kenya, South Africa, Nigeria, Cameroon and The Gambia have complained that their citizens have been lured to fight under false promises of work or educational opportunities.

articles.title: How Iliana Yotova won the presidential election in Bulgaria
articles.summary: Iliana Yotova won the presidential election in Bulgaria, promising to be a "president of peace." But the campaign showed how divided Bulgarians are about the war in Ukraine and drone attacks in the Black Sea.
articles.preview: November 2, 2026 Iliana Yotova won the presidential election in Bulgaria, promising to be a "president of peace." But the campaign showed how divided Bulgarians are about the war in Ukraine and drone attacks in the Black Sea. "We are choosing between war and peace," Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev told voters ahead of Sunday's presidential election runoff between incumbent President Iliana Yotova, who opposes military aid to Ukraine and favors dialogue with Russia, and former caretaker Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov, who is regarded as staunchly…
articles.body:
November 2, 2026

Iliana Yotova won the presidential election in Bulgaria, promising to be a "president of peace." But the campaign showed how divided Bulgarians are about the war in Ukraine and drone attacks in the Black Sea.

"We are choosing between war and peace," Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev told voters ahead of Sunday's presidential election runoff between incumbent President Iliana Yotova, who opposes military aid to Ukraine and favors dialogue with Russia, and former caretaker Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov, who is regarded as staunchly pro-European and pro-Ukrainian.

With these words, it was clear that Sunday's runoff had turned into a kind of referendum on the country's foreign policy and stance on the war in Ukraine.

Now that the official results are in and it is clear that Iliana Yotova won the election decisively by 57.6% to Gyurov's 39.5%, Radev claims that Bulgarians have chosen peace.

But is it really as simple as all that?

First-round surprise

When the presidential election campaign began in Bulgaria on September 25, there did not seem to be any doubt about the outcome: Iliana Yotova was well ahead in the polls on 44.5%. Gyurov, her main rival, trailed far behind on 26.1%.

Yotova was backed by both the prime minister and his ruling Progressive Bulgaria party, which won an absolute majority in the parliamentary election on April 19.

But the first round turned out to be much tighter than anticipated.

While Yotova got 34.8% of the vote in the first round, Gyurov was close behind on 31.95%, which meant that a runoff between the two was necessary.

Decisive victory, clear divide

While Yotova won the runoff convincingly, both the campaign and the outcome showed that the Bulgarian electorate is divided.

This division is both generational and geographical, explains Dimitar Ganev, sociologist and political scientist at the Trend market and electoral research agency.

"Younger voters — those aged between 18 and 40 — favor Gyurov. Those over 40 tend to prefer Yotova," Ganev told DW. "It also appears that Gyurov dominates in the capital, Sofia. In smaller regional cities, other towns and villages, Yotova dominates decisively," he said.

'President of peace'

This divide was also evident during the campaign.

While Andrey Gyurov relied mainly on social media for his campaign, Yotova chose to speak mostly to supporters of Progressive Bulgaria in closed venues.

At such events, the war in Ukraine was always high on the agenda.

"As long as I am president, and if you place your trust in me, not a single Bulgarian soldier will go to Ukraine," Yotova declared at an election rally on October 6 — even though according to the Bulgarian Constitution, only parliament (not the president) has the authority to send troops abroad or declare war.

Throughout the campaign, she referred to her opponents as "warmongers" and described herself as the "president of peace."

"We won because we talked to people about income and about peace," Yotova said after the election.

Russia's war in Ukraine a major campaign issue

In this, she is similar to Prime Minister Rumen Radev.

When it comes to Ukraine, Radev regularly speaks of the need for peace and avoids calling Russia an "aggressor." Both Radev and Yotova oppose military aid to Ukraine and criticize European leaders for not making sufficient efforts to engage with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Gyurov, on the other hand, has sharply criticized Russian aggression in Ukraine.

Appointed caretaker prime minister by Yotova in February, Gyurov in March signed a security cooperation agreement with Ukraine, provoking the disapproval of both Yotova and Radev.

The impact of drone attacks in the Black Sea

In the weeks leading up to the election, several ships in the Black Sea were hit by drones off the Bulgarian coast.

The European Council criticized Russia for the escalation, and the European Parliament called on the EU and its member states "to consider deploying an EU naval operation" there.

Prime Minister Radev, however, was not as equivocal, going no further than summoning the Russian ambassador and stating that "logic suggests that the outcome" of the attacks in the Black Sea "is to the advantage of the Russian Federation."

Just days before the runoff, he noted that "two ships were struck and sunk in Romanian territorial waters" after Romania had held Russia responsible for the attacks in the Black Sea.

"Many people think that once the aggressor is identified, the attacks will stop," he said, downplaying the Kremlin's responsibility. His remarks drew criticism from politicians and the media in Romania.

Yotova also did not name Russia as the perpetrator, instead saying during her campaign that she did not want to see "foreign flags in Bulgaria" — a clear reference to the Ukrainian flag, which has been displayed outside several institutions in Bulgaria as a sign of solidarity with the war-torn country.

How other voters voted

Most opposition parties, including the right-wing conservative GERB led by former long-serving Prime Minister Boyko Borisov, refused to field a candidate for the presidency, which is one reason why turnout on Sunday was less than 30%.

In the first round, the pro-Russian candidate Kostadin Kostadinov from the nationalist Vazrazhdane (Revival) party came third with 12.5% of the vote. According to Dimitar Ganev, around 70% of Vazrazhdane voters backed Yotova in the runoff.

To secure their support, Yotova targeted pro-Russian voters.

"Russia is by no means an enemy of Bulgaria," she said in a podcast interview just two days before the runoff, adding "Russia is part of our history, and I very much hope that it will be a key factor in the future security architecture across Europe, including for us."

In the days leading up to the vote, some of her supporters began claiming that the opposition was preparing a "Maidan," a reference to the Ukrainian revolution of 2014 that culminated in the ousting of President Viktor Yanukkovych, who had close ties to Moscow.

"All of Gyurov's lackeys are speaking openly about inevitable protests. They're using prime time to stir up a Maidan. Every single one of them," Sonya Momchilova, who was appointed to the media regulator by Radev, wrote on Facebook on Sunday.

Similar claims were made by both former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban and former Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic ahead of this year's elections in their countries.

Bulgaria in the EU and NATO

"This claim that Ms. Yotova will be a president of peace is directly linked to the incitement of a fear of war," said former Defense Minister Todor Tagarev, who was part of the committee that nominated Andrey Gyurov for president. "Bulgaria will be in a much worse position within Europe and NATO under her leadership," he said during a TV interview.

Dimitar Ganev, on the other hand, sees no threat to Bulgaria's commitment to the EU and NATO. "Over two-thirds of Bulgarians do not question the country's geopolitical orientation, and around two-thirds have a positive attitude towards the EU," he told DW.

But the positions of Radev and Yotova, which many view as ambivalent, mobilized both the pro-European camp and Eurosceptic voters, who, according to Ganev, make up around a third of the country's population.

According to Prime Minister Rumen Radev and President Iliana Yotova, the Bulgarian people chose peace in the presidential election. Nevertheless, the war continues.

Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan

articles.title: Ukraine’s new pocket-sized gadget turns Russian drones’ cameras against them
articles.summary: A Kyiv startup’s pocket-sized, 10-ounce receiver lets Ukrainian troops watch the video feeds of Russian drones, though Russian moves toward digital video and AI-guided drones that emit no signals could make the victory short-lived.
articles.preview: Ukrainian drone teams have a new way to spy on the drones that spy on them. A Kyiv equipment startup called CODE380 has been gaining attention for a pocket-sized receiver, the D·Vision SDR, that picks up live camera video from many Russian drones and shows it on a screen. articles.body:
Ukrainian drone teams have a new way to spy on the drones that spy on them. A Kyiv equipment startup called CODE380 has been gaining attention for a pocket-sized receiver, the D·Vision SDR, that picks up live camera video from many Russian drones and shows it on a screen.

Those drones send their video over the air without any scrambling, so anyone with the right receiver can watch along. A Ukrainian unit can see where a drone is heading and what its pilot is aiming at before it hits.

According to Defense News, the device is light, at about 10 ounces, which is less than half the weight of competing Ukrainian models, one of which weighs a couple of pounds.

It also listens on the radio channels Russia’s newer Molniya drones started using for video in June. Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov, a radio specialist who advises Ukraine’s president, said in a June Facebook post cited by Defense News that “most detectors don’t see these frequencies, or see them poorly.” He warned that putting too much trust in a detector could prove fatal.

Beskrestnov has also warned that digital video could one day replace analog, which would blind receivers like this one. The New York Times reported in August that some Molniyas are AI-guided, using Nvidia chips and emitting no signals.
