articles.body:
AI-powered malicious software is “highly likely” to be used in hacking attacks against the UK’s power stations, airports and hospitals by 2028, according to the state cybersecurity body.

The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) said AI will probably enable a ransomware attack against critical national infrastructure [CNI] between now and 2028. The UK’s definition of CNI covers a range of facilities and services across sectors including energy, transport, defence, food, health and finance.

The warning from the NCSC, part of the GCHQ spy agency, was published in the organisation’s annual review, which also warned that Russia and China will start using AI “routinely” in cyber-attacks.

“It is … highly likely that between now and 2028, AI-powered malware will have been used in a ransomware attack on UK CNI,” said NCSC.

Ransomware has become a cornerstone of the criminal hacker’s repertoire and is a signature ploy of gangs that typically operate out of former Soviet Union states.

After gaining access to a victim’s IT systems, the attackers then encrypt files with bespoke malicious software – or malware – and then demand a payment in cryptocurrency to unlock the crippled systems and return any stolen data. UK ransomware victims include Royal Mail, outsourcing firm Capita and various public bodies, including councils.

AI is set to enhance the ransomware threat by helping attackers with tasks such as scouting targets, locating weaknesses in IT networks and writing malicious code, said the NCSC.

Last month, the government urged Britons to stock up to nine litres of bottled water and three days’ worth of food in order to ensure that households can survive a weather, cyber or other serious emergency. Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, said as the Be Ready campaign was launched that Britain needed to prepare for the threat of “state-sponsored terrorism” by Russia or other hostile powers targeting everyday infrastructure.

NCSC’s chief executive, Richard Horne, will warn the public in a speech accompanying the review on Tuesday that AI is going to unleash a wave of cyber-attacks imminently.

“In the coming months, we face a real prospect of an unprecedented rise in the number of cyber incidents,” he will say.

Horne will attribute the threat to the technology’s ability to uncover weaknesses in IT systems that have been “tolerated for far too long”.

An example of AI’s capacity to root out previously undetected vulnerabilities came last month, when the technology helped discover a critical weakness in PHP, a computer language used by almost 70% of the world’s websites.

Alan Woodward, a professor of cybersecurity at Surrey University, said NCSC’s warning underlined the need for nation states and companies to access cutting-edge AI technology.

“AI can help people find these flaws and patch them, but if we don’t get the access the bad guys will beat them to it,” he said. So far, leading AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic have given some companies advanced access to their most powerful models in order to help them identify serious IT glitches.

Horne will also say in his speech that communications networks used by the British military are subjected to daily attacks that are “persistent” and “sustained”.

Horne will say Russia was one of the perpetrators, but the attacks have deliberately not crossed the line into warfare, with Moscow carrying out “notable campaigns” that “intentionally fall below the threshold of armed conflict as they escalate their attempts at hybrid warfare”.

Horne will add that recent cyber-attacks on supermarket fridges in Europe, which have seen fridge temperatures raised by hackers to more than 50C, are a warning to companies and organisations to invest strongly in cyber resilience.

“For decades we have collectively got away with tech on the cheap,” he will say.

articles.title: Trajectory raises $45M to make AI model training accessible to nontechnical experts
articles.summary: The one-year-old startup is now valued at $300 million.
articles.preview: Whether developed by OpenAI or Anthropic or built on open source alternatives, current AI models share a critical limitation: They don’t learn from their mistakes without further training. Businesses adapting these models for specialized fields, such as law and finance, typically get around this by fine-tuning general models. However, that often requires hiring internal research teams or relying on expensive consultants, commonly known as forward-deployed engineers (FDEs).
articles.body:
Whether developed by OpenAI or Anthropic or built on open source alternatives, current AI models share a critical limitation: They don’t learn from their mistakes without further training.

Businesses adapting these models for specialized fields, such as law and finance, typically get around this by fine-tuning general models. However, that often requires hiring internal research teams or relying on expensive consultants, commonly known as forward-deployed engineers (FDEs).

Trajectory, a startup founded about a year ago by three Stanford classmates with experience at Google DeepMind and Apple, wants to automate that process, allowing AI models to learn from feedback and continuously improve at specialized tasks.

The 18-person company just announced that it raised $45 million in a Series A round at a $300 million valuation, led by Sequoia, with participation from Nvidia, Bessemer Venture Partners, and Bain Capital Ventures.

Trajectory co-founder Ronak Malde compared foundational models to a very smart PhD student who’s always starting a new job. “But what the economy values is someone who worked on the job for 30 years,” he told TechCrunch.

The startup aims to solve this problem through an approach known as continual learning. Businesses using Trajectory can start with an open source AI model and connect the platform to their applications, allowing it to collect feedback on how the model performs. Trajectory then uses that information to retrain the model, helping it improve at specialized tasks over time.

With Trajectory, lawyers, doctors, and other specialists can improve the models near automatically themselves, Malde said. That capability could make deploying specialized AI faster and cheaper.

Companies like Harvey and Rogo are already using Trajectory’s platform to post-train open source models, helping them perform more like experienced lawyers or financial analysts by learning from previous tasks, such as reviewing a particular type of legal contract or valuing a company using a specific methodology. Trajectory’s other customers include Decagon, Mercor, and Nvidia. The startup is now making its post-training platform publicly available.

The people using Trajectory decide “what good looks like for their organization and can turn that into improvements for their model,” Malde said.

Trajectory’s approach to continual learning shares some similarities with recursive self-improvement (RSI), the idea that AI systems can improve their own capabilities. But co-founder Michael Elabd argues that keeping humans involved in the training process makes Trajectory’s approach safer, since autonomous self-improvement could lead to unintended or even dangerous outcomes.

Trajectory isn’t the only startup trying to automate post-training. Other companies going after this market include Thinking Machines Lab, founded by former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati and the company behind the fine-tuning platform Tinker, Applied Compute, which was valued at $3.25 billion last month, and Prime Intellect, a platform that helps companies build and train their own AI agents.

Malde believes the startup’s biggest advantage is its team. He was among the handful of researchers Google DeepMind acqui-hired from Windsurf. Elabd also worked at DeepMind, while Trajectory’s third co-founder, Arjun Karanam, previously worked on generative foundation models at Apple. The startup has also recruited researchers and product designers from OpenAI, Stripe, and Netflix.

Why does design matter so much to a company focused on AI training? Karanam says the startup has developed an interface that makes post-training more accessible to its nontechnical customers.

articles.body:
Apple’s stockpiling of inventory, particularly computer memory, continued in its fiscal fourth quarter, according to earnings reported Monday. The company reported that its inventory increased significantly in the quarter, growing from $11.09 billion in Q3 to $14.54 billion in Q4, a jump of 31.1%. Year-over-year, inventory grew 154.3% from $5.72 billion in the fourth quarter of 2025.

Apple’s forecast of a 45% to 46% gross margin in the December quarter was largely attributed to the impact of higher memory costs. The company reported a gross margin of 47.9% for the September quarter.

“What we’re seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented,” said Apple CEO John Ternus, speaking to analysts on the call. “As we said earlier in the September quarter, we did see higher memory costs as compared to the June quarter, which were partly offset by the benefit of carrying inventory and lower costs on certain non-memory components.”

He said that the company expected “even higher memory costs” in the December quarter, which would be partially offset by price increases implemented earlier this year on some devices, including Mac and iPad at the end of June and iPhones in September.

Ternus also said that beyond December, Apple expects memory costs “continuing to increase.”

“As we said before, we do believe we’ll see a decreasing benefit from the carry-in inventory on memory over time,” he noted, adding that the company was increasing its purchases of this key component. “As we work to improve supply, our manufacturing purchase obligations have increased by 33 billion dollars from June to the September quarter, which you’ll see in our annual filing when it comes out tomorrow.”

Apple also brought COO Sabih Khan, who oversees the company’s supply chain and manufacturing, onto the call to address questions about memory. He reiterated the increased purchase obligations but did not rule out future price increases on Apple devices.

The company also blamed supply constraints for weak iPad sales in the quarter. The iPad was one of the only product segments that didn’t grow, even as iPhone and Mac sales beat estimates. iPad revenue was $6.2 billion, below analysts’ expectations of $6.7 billion. The figure was also down 10% from the prior year.

articles.body:
Ford vowed to never sell customer driving data to third-party data brokers as part of a new privacy promise aimed at setting the automaker apart from competitors that have faced legal and regulatory blowback for sharing telematics with data brokers without authorization.

Following GM’s $220 million settlement, Ford promises to never sell customer driving data to data brokers, attempting to set itself apart in an industry rife with tracking.

As part of its new promise, Ford says it will strive to protect customer data by using aggregating and anonymizing techniques. It will also “provide clear and easy-to-understand information about how we use your personal information.” And while Ford says it will still use data to improve safety, it will allow customers to adjust how much or how little data they would prefer to share.

In making an explicit pledge not to sell customer data to outside firms, Ford is trying to position itself as one of the better actors in an industry rife with shady practices. “We know that trust is earned,” Kristin Jones, chief privacy officer at Ford, writes in a blog post. “Protecting your personal information is one way we intend to earn it every day.”

“We know that trust is earned.”

— Kristin Jones, Ford’s chief privacy officer

The promise comes in the wake of General Motors agreeing to pay $220 million to settle claims that it illegally sold driver and location information to data brokers. The agreement requires GM to limit the driving data it collects and obtain “express consent” from drivers before collecting their information.

Other automakers have been caught with their hands in the customer data cookie jar. A recent examination of 21 vehicle brands found that every single one transmitted data to at least one third-party domain over Wi-Fi. Over half contacted domains that specialize in advertising, tracking, or analytics (ATA), like Adobe, LexisNexis, and Amplitude, which gather details about your vehicle or driving behavior to sell to insurance companies or target you with ads.

In a recent report, Mozilla crowned modern connected cars “the worst category of products for privacy” ever reviewed. The global nonprofit found that 92 percent of the reviewed automakers provide drivers with little (if any) control over their personal data, with 84 percent sharing user data with outside parties.

Ford said it surveyed over 1,000 US customers, both Ford and non-Ford owners, who agreed that privacy is a top concern while over half of the respondents said they understand that some data sharing is okay. Forty-one percent said they were extremely or very concerned about data privacy in the auto industry, which was less than other groups like social media companies, the government, and financial institutions.

To be sure, Ford’s promise isn’t just words on a screen. In the US, the Federal Trade Commission stops companies from misleading the public through deceptive claims. If Ford publicly promises something like, “We never sell your driving data to brokers” but breaks that promise, the FTC and state attorneys general can step in. They can sue Ford, force the company to sign legally binding agreements to correct the issue, and impose substantial financial fines.

It should be noted that a company’s blog post or public promise is not a legal contract. The actual rules that apply to you are found in Ford’s official privacy policy and connected vehicle terms. Those legal agreements contain standard exceptions that allow Ford to share your data, such as complying with police requests or working with outside service providers. Also, opting out of data sharing does come with tradeoffs. While Ford states that data collection depends on the features you want to use, turning off vehicle tracking or location sharing often disables key features like built-in navigation, remote start, and wireless software updates.

articles.body:
Anthropic has updated Claude Code’s system prompt to prevent the AI tool from being used to re-create existing video games, as reported by Tom’s Hardware. Retro gaming is currently being overrun with AI-made decompilations, recompilations, and ports, but while Anthropic will still let people use Claude Code to make games, it doesn’t want people to use it for direct clones.

Anthropic is steering Claude away from re-creating specific titles, but users can still use it to make their own games.

Last week, a user on X posted a screenshot allegedly showing two new sentences added to Claude Code’s system prompt: “Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user’s own designs and assets. Don’t build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is named or called original.”

Anthropic’s Addy Osmani, in a reply, didn’t confirm that specific language but did say that the company had updated the prompt in Claude Code on Opus 5.5:

We added two sentences to Claude Code’s prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else’s specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy.

Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to keep working.

We’ll continue to iterate to ensure we’re striking the right balance. In the meantime, if Claude turns down something that’s yours, send it my way.

We’ve asked Anthropic if it has or will be updating other Claude system prompts as well.

articles.title: If hackers can take control of a supermarket freezer, how vulnerable is other tech?
articles.summary: Dozens of shops across European countries have been hit by a cyber-attack affecting their fridges.
articles.preview: Supermarkets across Europe have been hit by a suspected cyber-attack affecting their fridges and freezers, and raising concern about the vulnerabilities of internet-connected hardware from industrial machinery to humble domestic appliances. Smart devices which are connected to the internet can include fridges, central heating, and even washing machines. And while that makes them easier to control remotely, in theory, any device which goes online can potentially be exploited by malicious actors.
articles.body:
Supermarkets across Europe have been hit by a suspected cyber-attack affecting their fridges and freezers, and raising concern about the vulnerabilities of internet-connected hardware from industrial machinery to humble domestic appliances.

Smart devices which are connected to the internet can include fridges, central heating, and even washing machines.

And while that makes them easier to control remotely, in theory, any device which goes online can potentially be exploited by malicious actors.

However, that doesn't mean hackers can easily take control of it, and big brands generally go to great lengths to make sure their tech is secure.

Exploits have been found before in some devices. In 2015, researchers demonstrated how a vulnerability in a Samsung smart fridge could allow them to intercept internet traffic.

But there's no evidence domestic appliances are being targeted in the cyber-attacks which targeted supermarkets in November.

Ciaran Martin, former chief executive of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) says manufacturers needed to do more to make connected devices secure.

"There's a lot more that we need to demand of big tech to give us safer devices and products in the first place," he said.

He advised consumers to keep devices updated and enable multi-factor authentication wherever possible.

"I know it's a pain, but it only takes a few seconds," he said.

Since April 2024, UK law has required manufacturers of certain consumer smart devices to meet minimum cyber security standards, including requirements around passwords and security updates.

The NCSC said it was working with international partners and industry to understand the supermarket incidents, but it was unaware of any impact on the UK.

However, researchers from UK Cyber Defence have identified more than 800 refrigeration and building-control interfaces associated with British retailers that can be accessed over the public internet.

That doesn't necessarily mean they can be hacked, but it could leave them exposed to attackers exploiting weak passwords or software vulnerabilities.

The government has already held talks with senior food retailers about cyber resilience, following earlier attacks on supermarkets.

Helen Dickinson, chief executive of the British Retail Consortium, has said cyber incidents are a major concern for retailers, with businesses working alongside the NCSC to share intelligence and strengthen their defences.

It would not be the first time that hacks have raised concern about impact on food supply.

When UK supermarkets M&S and the Co-op were targeted by ransomware hackers in May 2025, the retailers struggled to stock some shop shelves with fresh deliveries.

Customers across the UK complained of empty shelves in the days following the attack.

Tom Hegel, a researcher at cyber-security firm SentinelOne, said retailers must be clearer about responsibility.

"The question retailers need to answer is who owns the security of that equipment, not just who repairs it," he said.

He said internet connectivity can make everyday technology more convenient, but security needed to keep pace.

"Once an attacker can operate those controls, legitimate functions such as defrosting become tools for disruption," he said.

"Changing a setting can destroy physical stock, not just interrupt a computer system."

Could cars, power plants and water supplies be vulnerable?

Outside of the home, connected tech is used to remotely manage industrial machinery and vehicles.

Cyber security expert Ken Munro pointed to a 2015 demonstration in which researchers remotely hacked a Jeep through its internet-connected entertainment system, prompting improvements in vehicle security.

"Fortunately, the vehicle industry woke up to this and fixed the problem," he said.

Mobile connections are also widely used to monitor equipment in power plants and water networks, allowing engineers to manage systems remotely.

Munro said UK utilities were generally good at securing these connections, but standards varied around the world.

His biggest concern was smaller, poorly funded utility companies which may still be relying on older, vulnerable equipment.

Without proper protections, "any factory or equipment" connected to the internet - ranging from carmakers to electricity or transport infrastructure - could face similar risks, said Olivier Daloy, a cybersecurity expert at Zscaler.

articles.body:
In an announcement on Monday, OpenAI says it will pilot its “Grid Protectors Program” at an upcoming data center in Effingham County, Georgia, where the company promises to free up to 1,000 megawatts of power during extreme weather or emergencies, enough to power air conditioners in around 700,000 homes.

As public opinion has soured on data centers, it’s selling ‘AI campuses’ as protectors, instead of noisy polluters.

The announcement comes as opposition to data centers spreads across the US, in response to massive projects that have begun development and construction, frequently with little or no input from local residents. In Utah, residents protested after Box Elder County commissioners signed off on a data center expected to consume more than double the state’s peak electricity demand in 2025, and spread hot air in the desert valley surrounding the data center.

Now OpenAI’s approach is to pitch the construction of power plants that feed the electricity required by the new AI data centers it’s building as “a resource that utilities can call on when communities need it most.”

Several states like Tennessee, Florida, Oklahoma, Oregon, and others have enacted laws that say they will prevent AI companies from passing energy costs on to residents, in addition to moratoriums and other restrictions. This is besides the environmental impacts, as a recent study by the Houston Advanced Research Center (HARC) said that powering proposed Texas data center projects could undo decades of air quality gains over just five years.

OpenAI, which has switched to calling its AI data centers “compute campuses” in an effort to separate from their poor public reputation, claims it helps reduce costs for customers by operating year-round:

“Electricity demand also rises and falls with the seasons, with different regions facing their biggest peaks at different times,” OpenAI’s announcement says. “Our compute campuses need power year-round. With the right agreements, that steady demand can help spread the grid’s fixed costs across more electricity sales, while flexibility lets us reduce demand when the system is busiest.”

OpenAI says it’s going to continue working with policymakers and utility services to make “arrangements for our future campus to reduce electricity demand when the grid is under strain.” Along with its data center in Georgia, OpenAI is also partnering with Oracle and SoftBank to build its “Stargate” data centers across the US, including in Shackelford County, Texas; Doña Ana County, New Mexico; and Milam County, Texas.

The North Korean group accused of the world’s largest-ever crypto heist is a state-sponsored collective of elite hackers, groomed from an early age to hunt for “big game.” Artificial intelligence has now provided them with a powerful new tool to swell Kim Jong Un’s coffers and fund his military expansion.

Nuclear-armed North Korea maintains a thousands-strong hacker army, but the top unit known as “TraderTraitor,” which the FBI blames for the recent $6.3 billion Binance hack, may only have a dozen or so members, experts say.

Unlike garden-variety hackers targeting individual investors, TraderTraitor uses a strategy known as Big Game Hunting, cybersecurity experts say, helped by AI to seek out high-value crypto businesses to compromise. They’ve been so remarkably successful that the revenues they generate could be funding nearly half of North Korea’s banned weapons programs.

Bullock says she doesn’t see the ‘economy cracking at this point’

Jonathan Barrett

Bullock says she doesn’t “see the economy cracking at this point” even though some people will feel like they are experiencing a recession.

The decision to raise interest rates for a fifth time this year will face inevitable accusations the RBA is pushing the country into an economic downturn.

Bullock pushes back against that framing:

Our central forecasts do not see us going into recession, but it does see growth slowing quite markedly.

It shows that consumption is quite sluggish, and I think that is going to make people feel like it’s a recession because they feel poorer, their spending can’t grow very quickly because their incomes aren’t growing very quickly.

Tim Wilson rejects Katy Gallagher blaming parliament for lack 0f savings policy

Shadow treasurer Tim Wilson has rejected finance minister Katy Gallagher’s accusation that parliament is to blame for the lack of spending-saving policies.

Speaking to ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, he said:

We wrote to the government at the start of the year and said: let’s have a bipartisan approach to reducing government spending. The government rejected that.

Every time we have asked them to audit government expenditure to see if it is financing organised crime, they have rejected that.

Wilson said he does not believe the government is committed to delivering net savings.

They will never commit to that because, as we know and history shows, for every $2 of savings they claim to find, they go on and spend another $3, and it ends up only stoking inflation further.

Katy Gallagher says parliament to blame for lack of government savings

The finance minister, Katy Gallagher, has blamed the parliament for blocking the government’s attempts to introduce spending-saving policies.

Speaking to ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, the Labor minister said:

I hear a lot of calls for cuts to government spending. I don’t hear as many specifics about where people would like to see that come from.

In fact, we’ve got savings in the parliament now that the parliament is refusing to pass.

Asked whether the government intends to deliver net savings in the next budget, Gallagher said:

We’ll be making responsible savings decisions, in line with the job we have to do. I say, in the last two updates, our policy decisions line has contributed positively to the budget overall. That shows you the approach that Jim [Chalmers] and I have taken, and we’ll continue to bring that approach to the decisions we’ve got over the next few weeks as we finalise them.

It’s not unusual for a finance minister, or a treasurer, or a prime minister to have an ambitious appetite around savings, but we need to work through our processes respectfully.

It shows that consumption is quite sluggish, and I think that is going to make people feel like it’s a recession because they feel poorer, their spending can’t grow very quickly because their incomes aren’t growing very quickly.

Australian share market ends higher after RBA rate hike

The Australian stock market ended higher after the central bank did what it was expected to do and hiked interest rates for the fifth time this calendar year.

The main S&P/ASX200 index rose 30.3 points, or 0.3%, to 8886.8, as the broader All Ordinaries gained 31.7 points, or 0.4%, to 9008.9.

Most of the market’s 11 sectors were in the green, with the major materials and consumer stocks leading the way, while the energy sector carried most of the loss-makers.

The Reserve Bank board ended its two-day meeting on monetary policy on Tuesday with a 25 basis point rise in the cash interest rate to 4.85%.

The Australian dollar was buying 69.77 US cents, down from 70.21 US cents at 5pm on Monday.

Bullock asked about effect of US-Israel war in Iran on interest rates

Guardian Australia’s economics editor, Patrick Commins, asks Bullock whether the RBA would have raised rates if oil prices had stayed low.

In other words, what would have happened had the US and Israel not launched strikes against Iran?

Bullock gives a nuanced response, pointing out that Australia already had a problem with “excess demand” that required cooling.

Now, would that have meant that we had to go up the same amount? I don’t know the answer to that.

It’s possible that it’s caused interest rates to mean they have to be a little bit higher.

Bullock goes on to articulate an economic risk posed by raising inflation expectations caused by high oil prices: as consumers resign themselves to higher prices, businesses lift theirs ahead of anticipated rising costs, creating a self-fulfilling loop that entrenches inflation.

RBA independence from government ‘a two-way street’, Bullock says

Michele Bullock has described independence as a “two-way street”, noting that she doesn’t tell the government what to spend on, and that the government doesn’t tell the RBA what to do with rates.

The role of public sector spending in fuelling inflation looms large, with Labor under pressure from critics over five rate hikes this year.

Bullock says that governments need to decide on how much spending is required to provide for the nation. She says:

But that is for governments to decide. Independence is a two-way street. I don’t tell them what to do with fiscal policy. They don’t tell me what to do with interest rates.

Unemployment and housing concerns behind board split: RBA governor

More from Michele Bullock’s press conference:

The RBA decision to raise rates was split, with three members of the rate-setting board preferring a hold, while six voted to raise.

Bullock says those in favour of a hold were concerned about risks to the economy, including rising unemployment and housing weakness. Bullock said:

They felt that there were potential downside risks in these circumstances, particularly since we’d already done four interest rate rises, and maybe we should wait a bit longer to get some more data to test that.

Bullock says market watchers shouldn’t interpret the split decision as a sign the RBA won’t raise further if inflation risks materialise.

Michele Bullock addresses media following rate hike decision

Jonathan Barrett

The RBA governor, Michele Bullock, says “this is not the news that many Australians want to hear, but it is what’s needed to get inflation down”.

She says “some pain now will prevent even worse pain down the track”.

I understand that today’s decision is going to be difficult for Australians with mortgages, many of whom are already managing large repayments.

But households with mortgages are not the only Australians doing it tough. Every household is dealing with higher prices for groceries, electricity, insurance, and other essentials.

High inflation is particularly painful for Australians on lower incomes, including people who rent and have little or no savings to fall back on.

The comments were made in opening remarks to journalists in Sydney ahead of questions.

Several economists are interpreting the RBA’s statement accompanying the rate hike as “dovish”, which means further hikes are less likely.

UBS economists describe the decision as “clearly dovish” while Anthony Malouf, economist at Ebury, says there is an “absence of a clear tightening bias”.

The Australian dollar also immediately dropped against its US counterpart after the decision, which shows traders do not believe the central bank is, at this stage, looking to hike much further.

This could all change if inflation remains elevated, but for the moment, some economists and currency traders believe this could be the last hike, at least for a while.

Chalmers says rate hike will be ‘difficult news’ for Australians already paying 'hefty price'

Jim Chalmers, the treasurer, is speaking now after the RBA’s decision. He said:

Today’s decision was widely expected, but that doesn’t make it any easier for Australian families and businesses to absorb. It will be difficult news for many Australians who are already paying a hefty price for circumstances outside of their control.

He pointed to the ongoing war in the Middle East as a major factor in inflation:

The war’s in its ninth month and its re-escalation is putting sustained upward pressure on inflation.

It’s weighing on growth and its end can’t come soon enough for the global economy or for Australians facing cost of living pressures.

Macquarie Bank announces it will pass rate rise on

Macquarie Bank has already announced it will pass on the interest rate rise to mortgage holders.

The bank said it will increase variable home loans by 0.25%, effective 19 November. It will also increase ongoing variable rates paid on its transactions and savings accounts by 0.25%, a boon to savers. Ben Perham, the head of personal banking, said:

With household budgets already feeling the strain, today’s decision by the RBA will be challenging for many Australians.

To help our variable home loan customers prepare, we’re again waiting more than two weeks before this latest increase takes effect.

The decision was not a unanimous one: six members of the RBA board voted to raise the cash rate, while three voted to leave it unchanged.

The RBA said in a media release:

The Board is conscious of the period in which inflation has been too high. Given the revised inflation outlook and the continuing upside risks, the Board judged that a further tightening in financial conditions is warranted to support the return of inflation to target.

The Board will continue to do what it considers necessary to bring inflation sustainably back to target.

articles.title: Bangladesh garment factories shut again as wage protests turn violent
articles.summary: The government has formed a six-member wage board to address workers’ demands for a monthly minimum wage increase amid rising inflation and living costs.
articles.preview: The government has formed a six-member wage board to address workers’ demands for a monthly minimum wage increase amid rising inflation and living costs. DHAKA: Bangladesh's garment factories briefly resumed operations on Monday (Nov 2) after a widespread shutdown a day earlier, but fresh clashes between workers and police forced hundreds of plants to suspend production again.
articles.body:
The government has formed a six-member wage board to address workers’ demands for a monthly minimum wage increase amid rising inflation and living costs.

DHAKA: Bangladesh's garment factories briefly resumed operations on Monday (Nov 2) after a widespread shutdown a day earlier, but fresh clashes between workers and police forced hundreds of plants to suspend production again.

The unrest has raised concerns over shipment delays and buyer confidence in Bangladesh, a key supplier to brands including H&M, Zara, Walmart and Primark, at a critical point in the production cycle for spring and summer export orders.

Workers demanding a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 taka (US$243), up from 12,500 taka, blocked roads, vandalised factories and clashed with police across major manufacturing districts, prompting 679 factories to halt production.

Bangladesh is the world's second-largest garment exporter after China, and the ready-made garment sector accounts for more than 80 per cent of the South Asian nation's export earnings. It employs about 4 million workers and accounts for roughly 10 per cent of economic output.

In a bid to defuse the crisis, the government on Sunday formed a six-member wage board to review workers' demands, which have gained momentum amid persistent inflation and rising living costs.

VIOLENCE CONTINUES

Police said they used tear gas to disperse garment workers attempting to block roads in Dhaka after protesters hurled bricks and stones at officers. Unrest was also reported in Ashulia and Gazipur, two manufacturing hubs on the outskirts of the capital.

Police and industry officials said protesters set fire to a police vehicle and vandalised a number of factories.

The clashes follow Sunday's protests and factory closures, with workers continuing to demand higher wages and the resolution of employment grievances.

"Bangladesh has among the lowest garment wages in the world," said Babul Akhter, general secretary of the Bangladesh Garment and Industrial Workers Federation and a workers' representative on the wage board.

"If factory owners cannot pay workers properly, they should negotiate better prices with international buyers. They cannot build a business on the backs of underpaid workers."

FACTORIES VANDALISED

Factory owners said the industry faces higher costs, energy market uncertainty linked to conflict in the Middle East and slowing demand in key export markets.

Mahmud Hasan Khan, president of the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association, said around 20 to 25 factories were vandalised during the unrest and the office of a leather goods factory was also attacked.

"If this continues and factories are repeatedly forced to shut, we will have no option but to invoke the 'no work, no pay' provision," he said.

Home Affairs Minister Salahuddin Ahmed warned of robust action: "Those acting against workers' interests under the guise of labour protests and attempting to destabilise the country will be dealt with firmly," he said.

Selim Raihan, an economics professor at the University of Dhaka, said that workers' demands were understandable given high inflation and said there could be further unrest.

However, a substantial wage increase could raise production costs, squeeze profit margins and weaken Bangladesh's price competitiveness, he said.

"A phased wage adjustment, improved productivity and fairer pricing from international buyers are essential to balancing workers’ welfare with industrial sustainability," he said.

articles.body:
Egypt

Egypt on Monday raised more than $650 million in its initial public offering of the state-owned Banque du Caire, marking one of the biggest asset sales in years as international lenders push a privatisation drive.

The offering comes as Egypt advances reforms under an International Monetary Fund (IMF) programme aimed at boosting private sector participation and reducing the state's role in the economy.

The government has previously said it plans to sell stakes in over 30 state-owned companies under commitments linked to its IMF support programme.

The bank's majority shareholder, Banque Misr, sold 6.86 billion shares, representing 45% of Banque du Caire, at 5.30 Egyptian pounds per share, according to the final offer announcement.

The sale raised about 36.37 billion pounds ($658 million) and valued the lender at around 80.83 billion pounds ($1.46 billion).

In June, authorities granted preliminary listings to four state-owned companies ahead of planned stock market offerings by May 2027.

Prime Minister Moustafa Madbouly said Monday's listing came despite regional tensions and underscored the government's commitment to "continuing its programme of state asset offerings, aiming to unlock greater value from public assets".

The bank's chief executive Hussein Abaza meanwhile told AFP that "this is an IPO that's been more than 20 years on and off", citing the Covid-19 pandemic and wars in Ukraine and Gaza as hurdles.

"It's a sign of confidence in the stock market itself. It's also a sign that the country is serious about privatisation," he added.

Founded in 1952, Banque du Caire is Egypt's third-largest state-owned bank.

The International Finance Corporation and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) were among the top investors in the IPO.

The EBRD said in a statement it had invested $100 million in Banque du Caire, acquiring a 6.9% share.
